reconnaissance_summary.censorship_and_self_censorship: The notebook reports intimidation, surveillance, blocked outlets, self-censorship, and DSA-based prosecution, creating high underreporting risk for security-force abuse, procurement, appointments, nuclear safety, and personal finances.
chapter_specific_biases: 1B: formal treaty and regulatory records exceed operational and personal nuclear-risk evidence.
2B: refugee and political-violence reporting exceeds military-restraint and procurement evidence.
3B: complaint suppression and incomplete denominators limit inference from abuses and local zeros.
4B: inherited 2018 conditions and disputed shutdown reports require temporal and attribution caution.
5B: macro and programme sources weakly identify distribution, completion, appointments, and personal decisions.
6B: outcomes and humanitarian reports leave affordability, quality, neutrality, and durability weakly observed.
8B: programmes and outcomes do not establish ruler-specific execution or adaptation.
reconnaissance_summary.complaint_volume_interpretation: Visible NGO and refugee complaints may overrepresent abuses, while intimidation, self-censorship, closed institutions, and weak investigations suppress complaints. Absence of complaints is not evidence of absence.
reconnaissance_summary.criticism_possible: Criticism was possible through UN bodies, NGOs, press-freedom groups, diplomatic reporting, specialist assessments, and international media, but the notebook documents meaningful intimidation and self-censorship.
reconnaissance_summary.duplicate_event_risk: Repeated HRW, Freedom House, RSF, UN, World Bank, IMF, U.S., and UK reporting may overlap. Same-source splits were retained only for distinct claims; family counts are not event counts.
reconnaissance_summary.inherited_conditions_shocks_and_authorit: Hasina held formal prime-ministerial executive responsibility under Articles 55–56, while attribution was constrained by cabinet, parliament, security institutions, courts, donors, subnational actors, and humanitarian partners. COVID recovery, Ukraine-related inflation and reserves pressure, climate and flood shocks, Myanmar spillover, Rohingya displacement, and inherited trajectories shaped 2022.
languages_and_archives_searched: English-language official, intergovernmental, NGO, specialist, media, and comparative-assessment sources supplied in the notebook.
Bangladesh legal, government, treaty, and policy records.
reconnaissance_summary.official_statistics_reliability: Local indicators and official or programme statistics are used as outcomes, exposure, or baseline context, not direct ruler evidence. Nominal GDP changes require a real-value caveat; self-reported programme completion and humanitarian figures have scope limitations.
reconnaissance_summary.relevant_denominators: The notebook supplies UCDP, SIPRI, DSA, political-event, extrajudicial-death, disappearance, education-participation, refugee-reach, and service-level denominators, while explicitly noting incomplete nationwide incident, distributional, and remedy denominators.
reconnaissance_summary.safe_reporting_channels: UN mechanisms and agencies, international NGOs, diplomatic reports, foreign-government reports, international financial institutions, specialist assessments, and international media were comparatively safer channels; domestic reporting remained constrained.
reconnaissance_summary.source_concentration: Chapters 3B and 4B have the greatest source diversity. Chapters 1B, 5B, 6B, and 8B rely more on intergovernmental and structured sources. Reused source families are not treated as independent corroboration.

resource_index.claim: OHCHR found DSA provisions vague and overbroad, with arbitrary-application risk, harsh penalties, and chilling effects.
Freedom House reported harassment of opposition, critical media, and civil society, weak due process, and security-force abuses with near impunity.
Freedom House recorded more than 2,200 DSA charges from January 2020 to February 2022, including journalists, with many cases filed by Awami League activists against critics.
RSF reported a hostile media environment, warrantless DSA searches and arrests, compelled source disclosure, and editorial self-censorship.

After opposition protests began on 22 August 2022, clashes involving police, BNP supporters, and Awami League supporters caused at least four deaths and hundreds of injuries; HRW characterized the campaign as a crackdown.
HRW reported December 2022 restrictions and police action against BNP campaign activity as elections approached.

Bangladesh’s Election Commission issued a September 2022 roadmap identifying 14 challenges including administrative neutrality, black money, muscle power, law and order, and public confidence in electronic voting.
Access Now/#KeepItOn reporting cited six Bangladesh internet shutdowns in 2022, reportedly around BNP rallies; government and BTRC denied issuing shutdown instructions.
The U.S. religious-freedom report recorded constitutional equality guarantees alongside minority complaints about harassment, violence, and insufficient punishment.
BTI reported executive concentration, Article 70 party discipline, weak parliamentary checks, executive judicial influence, and politically influenced judicial recruitment and promotion.
AP reported Hasina-government India engagement, development-project inaugurations, water-sharing and other agreements, and regional-security concerns.
